title: Beyond the Clipboard: The Delicate Art of Lesson Observation Feedback
author: Dario Emanuele
summary: Emanuele argues that feedback after a lesson observation is fundamental to teacher growth and wellbeing, yet giving it well is a delicate science that, done badly, can damage a colleague's practice for years. Observers hold immense power and must resist the golden-rule error of telling a colleague to copy-paste a strategy that works in their own room, because teaching is context-dependent, like a complex equation with dozens of shifting variables. He then sets out five "blind spots" of the observer, forgetting the observed teacher's cognitive load and memory, stating opinions as facts, dismissing the "unorthodox," enforcing dogmatic policies, and overwriting the domain expert, each paired with a practical fix rooted in inquiry, curiosity, and humility.
points: Feedback is fundamental to teacher growth and wellbeing, and experienced teachers need it as much as trainees, because there is no single method that works for all students.
Giving feedback badly can have detrimental, years-long effects, like embedding a misconception in a student; observers must respect the power they hold.
The golden rule: you cannot take a practice that works in your own classroom and tell a colleague to copy-paste it, teaching must be adapted to context.

Five observer blind spots, the forgetting curve (memory/cognitive load), assumption over inquiry, dismissing the unorthodox, dogmatic policies, and overwriting the domain expert, each degrade feedback.
Good coaching, asking questions, respecting context, managing cognitive load, builds confident teachers; poor feedback turns the process into a mock trial with prosecutor and defendant.
quotes: Giving feedback is deeply delicate work. If it is not done properly, or if it is delivered in a shallow, prescriptive way, it can have severely detrimental effects on the career of the observed teacher, effects that can last for years.
You cannot just take a practice that works well in your own classroom and tell your colleague to copy-paste it into theirs. Teaching has never worked like that.

Teaching is like a complex algebraic equation with dozens of shifting variables. A strategy that works wonders with a top-set Year 11 class on a Tuesday morning might cause chaos in a bottom-set Year 8 class on a windy Friday afternoon.
Sometimes, the observed teacher looks confused or hesitant, and the observer makes the fatal mistake of assuming the teacher didn’t know what they were doing. In reality, it’s just a memory problem!
These are brilliant strategies (I use them constantly!), but they are tools, not tyrants.
But if you do not deliver your feedback properly, the whole process degrades into a mock trial. The observer becomes the prosecutor, and the observed teacher becomes the defensive defendant.
